How Marketing Teams Actually Use AI Tools

By lowob · 11 June 2026 · Updated 10 November 2026 · 4-minute read · Growth / AI

AI works best in marketing when it helps people read, organize, draft and check real work. The problem starts when teams mistake more output for more customer understanding.

A few years into widespread use, AI tools in marketing teams have stopped being a novelty and become a set of habits. The habits are more specific and less dramatic than the early demonstrations suggested. Here is what the work actually looks like.

The jobs AI does well

Research and synthesis. Reading call transcripts, support tickets, reviews, and competitor pages, and pulling out patterns: the words customers use, the objections that recur, the claims competitors make. This can be useful because the source material already exists but teams often lack time to read it closely.

First drafts and variants. Turning a brief, a transcript, or an approved article into a first draft, a set of headlines, a social adaptation, an email sequence, or a version for a different audience. Fast, competent, and only as good as the source material.

Structured extraction. Converting unstructured notes into fields: objections, next steps, account details, campaign results. Reduces the administrative tax on people who talk to customers.

Analysis assistance. Explaining a data set, spotting anomalies in a report, drafting the query, comparing two periods. Not a replacement for someone who understands the numbers, but a faster path for them.

Quality control. Checking copy against a voice guide, a claims library, a compliance list, or a banned-words list. Helpful for routine checks, provided the rules and source facts are current.

What this looks like in practice

In an agency-published case study, DEPT describes building a custom AI agent with a major airline's content team. It checks incoming work tickets for missing information and broken links, estimates task complexity, and suggests metadata and tracking identifiers. DEPT reports that the project reduced manual ticket validation time by about two-thirds, though the performance figures are the agency's own account rather than an independent audit.

The useful lesson isn't that the agent replaced editorial judgement. DEPT says the team first mapped the content workflow, identified more than 20 potential opportunities and prioritized three repetitive tasks. Content managers remained involved in the design and use of the system. That is a much more realistic model than turning over campaign strategy to an autonomous content generator.

Where AI needs human judgment

AI can produce a polished argument without knowing which position a company should actually take. Original points of view still require people who understand the market, can weigh evidence and are prepared to be accountable for their conclusions. The same goes for facts and public claims: every important number, product capability and regulatory statement needs verification before it is published.

Automated outreach and public replies create a different risk. A plausible but incorrect message can reach a customer or regulator before anyone notices. And a team that replaces real customer conversations with AI summaries may lose the direct observations that make its strategy useful. The best role for AI is to prepare and test material, not replace the decisions or relationships behind it.

How a small team should set it up

Start with a shared, maintained source of truth: the company's products, approved claims, customer language, competitors and editorial standards. Then choose a few recurring tasks with clear inputs and outputs, such as turning customer calls into CRM notes or reviewing copy against an approved claims library.

Set a review rule before automating publication. Routine formatting might need a light check, while public claims or sensitive material may require an owner or legal reviewer. Store approved outputs so each new task builds on what the team already learned.

Honest expectations

The potential gains are meaningful: a small team can prepare research, drafts and administration faster. The gains are also bounded: the work that creates value, deciding what the company believes, talking to customers, choosing where to look, still takes people. Teams that use AI to do more of the second kind of work with the time saved on the first get ahead. Teams that use it to produce more output at the same quality mostly become louder.

lowob takeaways

  • Use AI on repeatable preparation and quality-control jobs before automating outward-facing decisions.
  • Connect every draft to approved product facts and customer evidence.
  • Make a human accountable for public claims, creative direction and publication.

Sources and notes

DEPT, Accelerating Content Management With a Custom AI Agent. Agency case study on an airline's content operations, describing validation, task sizing and SEO metadata automation. Numbers are DEPT-reported, not independently verified.

Anthropic, Introducing Agent Skills. Background on packaging repeatable instructions and resources.
